notes.meaning: God gave a message to Jeremiah during the tenth year of King Zedekiah's rule in Judah. This was the eighteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. Jerusalem was in deep trouble, only one year away from its final destruction.

The Babylonian army was surrounding Jerusalem and cutting off its food and supplies. King Zedekiah had locked Jeremiah up in the palace guardhouse to keep him from speaking freely. Even in prison, Jeremiah had an open courtyard where visitors could still come to see him.

King Zedekiah asked Jeremiah angrily why he kept preaching bad news. Jeremiah had warned everyone that the Lord was handing Jerusalem over to the king of Babylon. Instead of repenting of his sins, Zedekiah punished the prophet for telling the truth.

Jeremiah told the king that he would not escape from the enemy army. Zedekiah would be captured and brought right before the Babylonian king to look him in the eye and hear his judgment. This warned the proud king that he could not hide from the consequences of his rebellion.

Jeremiah warned that Zedekiah would be dragged away to Babylon and stay there until God decided his end. Fighting against the Babylonian soldiers was completely useless because the Lord was no longer fighting for Judah. The nation had to accept God's righteous discipline.

Jeremiah began to explain what God told him just before a family member arrived. The Lord spoke to him in advance so he would know exactly what to do. God often prepares His servants before testing their faith.

The Lord told Jeremiah that his cousin Hanamel would come and ask him to buy a family field in Anathoth. Under biblical law, the nearest relative had the first right and duty to buy family land to keep it from passing to strangers. Even though the enemy already controlled that land, God told Jeremiah the offer was coming.

Hanamel came to the prison courtyard just as the Lord had said, asking Jeremiah to buy the field. When his cousin showed up with that exact request, Jeremiah knew for certain that this was God's will. Seeing God's word come true in daily life strengthened the prophet's faith.

Jeremiah agreed to the sale and weighed out seventeen pieces of silver for his cousin. Buying land that was already occupied by enemy soldiers looked like throwing money away. Yet Jeremiah paid the price willingly because he trusted what God had promised.

Jeremiah completed every legal requirement by writing out the deed, sealing it, calling in witnesses, and weighing the silver on scales. He did not cut corners simply because he was in prison or because the city was under attack. God's people honor the Lord by doing ordinary business with honesty and care.

Jeremiah took two copies of the legal deed of purchase. One copy was sealed up with the official terms and conditions, while the second copy was left open for anyone to inspect. This custom protected the original record while letting people check the facts at any time.

Jeremiah handed the deeds to his trusted assistant Baruch in front of his cousin, the witnesses, and everyone sitting in the courtyard. Doing this in public made sure there would be no doubt about the purchase later on. It turned the private business deal into a public sign for all the people.

In front of all the witnesses, Jeremiah ordered Baruch to place both deeds into a clay jar so they would last for a very long time. Clay jars kept paper and scrolls safe from moisture, rot, and fire during war. This showed that the documents would still be needed long after the coming destruction.

The Lord explained the true meaning of the purchase. Even though the land was about to be ruined and the people carried off to Babylon, God promised that houses, fields, and vineyards would be bought again in Judah. God's promise gave the people hope that the exile would not last forever.

Once the legal papers were safely handed to Baruch, Jeremiah began to pray. He obeyed God's command to buy the field, but he still struggled to understand how God's promises of judgment and restoration fit together. When we are troubled by things we cannot understand, prayer is the best place to turn.

Jeremiah began his prayer by praising God as the Maker of heaven and earth through His great power. Because God created everything out of nothing, no problem is too hard for Him to solve. Remembering God's power helps quiet our fears when life seems impossible.

Jeremiah praised the Lord for His deep mercy toward thousands of people, while also acknowledging that God punishes sin across generations. God is the Almighty Lord of Hosts, who rules over every power in heaven and earth. He is both perfectly loving and perfectly holy in all His judgments.

differ.view: God punishes children when they share their parents' sinful nature, partly by leaving them without the grace of His Spirit.
God punishes children for family sins only when those children actively choose to copy and continue their parents' wickedness.

notes.meaning: God makes wonderful plans and has the full power to carry them out. His eyes watch every person on earth, seeing both the good and the bad. In the end, He will give each person the proper reward or punishment for how they lived.

Jeremiah reminded God of the mighty signs and miracles He performed in Egypt to rescue His people. The fame of those great acts had never faded, being remembered by Israel and other nations down to Jeremiah's day. God's past faithfulness reminds His people that He is still worthy of their trust.

God brought Israel out of slavery with ten plagues, mighty power, and terrifying judgment against their oppressors. The Israelites did not rescue themselves by their own strength or wisdom. Their freedom came entirely from God's outstretched arm.

God kept the solemn promise He made to Abraham and the fathers by giving the Israelites the land of Canaan. It was a rich and fruitful country, full of good things to eat and drink. Israel received this wonderful home purely as a gift from God's grace.
